The children can do with nothing less than the Father; they need the infinite one. Beyond all wherein the poor intellect can descry order; beyond all that the rich imagination can devise; beyond all that hungriest heart could long, fullest heart thank for﻿—beyond all these, as the heavens are higher than the earth, rise the thought, the creation, the love of the God who is in Christ, his God and our God, his Father and our Father.
Ages before the birth of Jesus, while, or at least where yet even Moses and his law were unknown, the suffering heart of humanity saw and was persuaded that nowhere else lay its peace than with the first, the last, the living one:﻿—
O that thou woudest hide me in the grave,﻿ ﻿… and remember me!﻿ ﻿… Thou shalt call, and I will answer thee: thou wilt have a desire to the work of thine hands.

===Chinese===

孩子们少于父便不能度日；他们需要那无限者。越过贫乏智力所能辨认秩序的一切；越过丰富想象所能构想的一切；越过最饿的心所能慕、最满的心所能谢的一切——越过这一切，如天之高于地，升起那在基督里之神的思念、创造与爱——他的神、我们的神，他的父、我们的父。
在耶稣出生之前的诸世代，当——或至少在——连摩西（Moses）和他的律法都还不为人知的地方，人类受苦的心看见并被劝服：它的平安不在别处，只在首先的、末后的、存活的那里：——
惟愿你把我藏在阴间……记念我！……你呼叫，我便回答；你手所做的，你必渴望。

### The Voice of Job / 约伯的声音
===Original===

> “O that thou wouldest hide me in the grave, that thou wouldest keep me secret, until thy wrath be past, that thou wouldest appoint me a set time, and remember me! If a man die, shall he live again? all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come. Thou shalt call, and I will answer thee: thou wilt have a desire to the work of thine hands.”

===Chinese===

> “惟愿你把我藏在阴间，把你隐瞒了，直到你的怒气过去；愿你为我定了日期，记念我！人若死了岂能再活呢？我只要在我一切争战的日子，等我被释放的时候来到。你呼叫，我便回答；你手所做的，你必渴望。”

===Original===

The book of Job seems to me the most daring of poems: from a position of the most vantageless realism, it assaults the very citadel of the ideal! Its hero is a man seated among the ashes, covered with loathsome boils from head to foot, scraping himself with a potsherd. Sore in body, sore in mind, sore in heart, sore in spirit, he is the instance-type of humanity in the depths of its misery﻿—all the waves and billows of a world of adverse circumstance rolling free over its head. I would not be supposed to use the word “humanity” either in the abstract, or of the mass concrete; I mean the humanity of the individual endlessly repeated: Job, I say, is *the human being*﻿—a centre to the sickening assaults of pain, the ghastly invasions of fear: these, one time or another, I presume, threaten to overwhelm every man, reveal him to himself as enslaved to the external, and stir him up to find some way out into the infinite, where alone he can rejoice in the liberty that belongs to his nature. Seated in the heart of a leaden despair, Job cries aloud to the Might unseen, scarce known, which yet he regards as the God of his life. But no more that of a slave is his cry, than the defiance of Prometheus hurled at Jupiter from his rock. He is more overwhelmed than the Titan, for he is in infinite perplexity as well as pain; but no more than in that of Prometheus is there a trace of the cowardly in his cry. Before the Judge he asserts his innocence, and will not grovel﻿—knowing indeed that to bear himself so would be to insult the holy. He feels he has not deserved such suffering, and will neither tell nor listen to lies for God.
Prometheus is more stonily patient than Job. Job is nothing of a Stoic, but bemoans himself like a child﻿—a brave child who seems to himself to suffer wrong, and recoils with horror-struck bewilderment from the unreason of the thing. Prometheus has to do with a tyrant whom he despises, before whom therefore he endures with unbewailing unsubmission, upheld by the consciousness that he is fighting the battle of humanity against an all but all-powerful Selfishness: endurance is the only availing weapon against him, and he will endure to the ever-delayed end!

===Chinese===

《约伯记》（the book of Job）在我看来是最大胆的诗：从最无险可据的现实主义阵地出发，它直攻理想本身的城堡！它的主角是一个坐在炉灰中的人，从头到脚长了可憎的毒疮，拿瓦片刮身体。身体痛、心思痛、心痛、灵里痛，他是人类在悲惨深处的一个典型——一个逆境的世界、它一切的波浪洪涛自由滚过头顶。我不要人以为我用“人类”一词是在抽象或集合意义上；我指的是那无尽重复的个体之人：约伯，我说，*就是那人*——是疼痛之令人作呕的攻击、恐惧之可畏侵入的一个中心：这些，我想，迟早威胁着要淹没每一个人，把他作为一个受制于外物者启示给他自己，并激动他去寻找某种出路、进入那无限——唯有在那里他能以他本性所属的自由欢然自得。坐在铅灰绝望的心中，约伯向那看不见、几乎不认识、却仍看为他生命之神的大能大声呼喊。但他的呼喊不再是奴隶的，正如普罗米修斯（Prometheus）从他的磐石上掷向朱庇特的那份蔑视。他比那提坦更被压倒，因为他既在痛中、也在无限的困惑中；但他的呼喊里没有一丝怯懦，不比普罗米修斯的呼喊里更多。在审判者面前他声称自己无辜，不肯匍匐——实在知道那样自持正是侮辱圣洁。他觉得他没有配受这样的苦，就既不为神说谎、也不听谎言。
普罗米修斯比约伯更石头般忍耐。约伯全不是斯多葛派，倒像个孩子那样哀叹——一个勇敢的孩子，自觉受了冤屈，带着惊骇的迷惘从这事的无理中退缩。普罗米修斯对付的是他所鄙夷的暴君，因此在暴君面前他以不哀诉的不屈忍受，支撑他的是这意识：他在为人类打一场对抗那几乎全能的自私的仗：对他，忍耐是唯一奏效的武器，他要忍到那永远迟延的尽头！

===Original===

Job, on the other hand, is the more troubled because it is He who is at the head and the heart, who is the beginning and the end of things, that has laid his hand upon him with such a heavy torture that he takes his flesh in his teeth for pain. He cannot, will not believe *him* a tyrant; but, while he pleads against his dealing with himself, loves him, and looks to him as the source of life, the power and gladness of being. He dares not think God unjust, but not therefore can he allow that he has done anything to merit the treatment he is receiving at his hands. Hence is he of necessity in profoundest perplexity, for how can the two things be reconciled? The thought has not yet come to him that that which it would be unfair to lay upon him as punishment, may yet be laid upon him as favour﻿—by a love supreme which would give him blessing beyond all possible prayer﻿—blessing he would not dare to ask if he saw the means necessary to its giving, but blessing for which, once known and understood, he would be willing to endure yet again all that he had undergone. Therefore is he so sorely divided in himself. While he must not think of God as having mistaken him, the discrepancy that looks like mistake forces itself upon him through every channel of thought and feeling. He had nowise relaxed his endeavour after a godly life, yet is the hand of the God he had acknowledged in all his ways uplifted against him, as rarely against any transgressor!﻿—nor against him alone, for his sons and daughters have been swept away like a generation of vipers! The possessions, which made him the greatest of all the men of the east, have been taken from him by fire and wind and the hand of the enemy! He is poor as the poorest, diseased as the vilest, bereft of the children which were his pride and his strength! The worst of all with which fear could have dismayed him is come upon him; and worse now than all, death is denied him! His prayer that, as he came naked from the womb, so he may return naked and sore to the bosom of the earth, is not heard; he is left to linger in self-loathing, to encounter at every turn of agonized thought the awful suggestion that God has cast him off! He does not deny that there is evil in him; for﻿—“Dost thou open thine eyes upon such an one,” he pleads, “and bringest *me* into judgment with *thee*?”

===Chinese===

约伯则相反，更受搅扰，因为向他下手的那位，是居于首、居于心、是万事的始与终的那位，下手如此沉重，使他咬牙切齿地痛。他不能、也不肯信*他*是暴君；但当他抗辩他对己的对待时，他爱他，仰望他作生命的源头、存有的能力与喜乐。他不敢想神不义，但也不能因此承认自己作了什么配受他手中这种对待的事。因此他必在最深的困惑里，因为两件事怎能调和？那念头还没有来到他心里：那作为刑罚加在他身上便不公平的事，作为恩宠仍可能加在他身上——借一种至高的爱，要给他超出一切可能祷告的福——那福若让他看见赐下它所需的手段，他不敢求，但一经认识明白，他就甘愿把他所经历的一切再受一遍。所以他里面如此剧烈地分裂。他既不可把神想成看错了人，那貌似错误的分歧又借每一条思想与情感的渠道逼到他面前。他对敬虔生活的追求分毫未曾松懈，然而他所凡事承认的神，手却起来攻击他，罕见地如对任何一个_过犯者！——还不止他一人：他的儿女像一窝毒蛇之代那样被扫去！使他成为东方至大之人的产业，被火、风和敌手的手夺去！他贫穷如最穷的，患病如最卑贱的，失去了他引为骄傲与力量的儿女！惧怕所能惊吓他的最坏之事都临到了他；而如今比一切都坏的，是死也不被准许！他祷告说，既赤身出于母胎，愿他赤身而痛地归回大地的怀抱，却不蒙垂听；他被撇下苟延于自厌中，在痛苦思想的每一转弯处迎面撞上那可畏的暗示：神已丢弃他！他不否认自己里面有恶；因为——“这样的人你岂要睁眼看他吗？还叫他来*同你*受审判（the judgment）吗？”

===Original===

but he does deny that he has been a wicked man, a doer of the thing he knew to be evil: he does deny that there is any guile in him. And who, because he knows and laments the guile in himself, will dare deny that there was once a Nathanael in the world? Had Job been Calvinist or Lutheran, the book of Job would have been very different. His perplexity would then have been﻿—how God being just, could require of a man more than he could do, and punish him as if his sin were that of a perfect being who chose to do the evil of which he knew all the enormity. For me, I will call no one Master but Christ﻿—and from him I learn that his quarrel with us is that we will not do what we know, will not come to him that we may have life. How endlessly more powerful with men would be expostulation grounded, not on what they have done, but on what they will not do!
Job’s childlike judgment of God had never been vitiated and perverted, to the dishonouring of the great Father, by any taint of such low theories as, alas! we must call the popular: explanations of God’s ways by such as did not understand *Him*, they are acceptable to such as do not care to know him, such as are content to stand afar off and stare at the cloud whence issue the thunders and the voices; but a burden threatening to sink them to Tophet, a burden grievous to be borne, to such as would arise and go to the Father. The contradiction between Job’s idea of the justice of God and the things which had befallen him, is constantly haunting him; it has a sting in it far worse than all the other misery with which he is tormented; but it is not fixed in the hopelessness of hell by an accepted explanation more frightful than itself. Let the world-sphinx put as many riddles as she will, she can devour no man while he waits an answer from the world-redeemer. Job refused the explanation of his friends because he knew it false; to have accepted such as would by many in the present day be given him, would have been to be devoured at once of the monster. He simply holds on to the skirt of God’s garment﻿—besieges his door﻿—keeps putting his question again and again, ever haunting the one source of true answer and reconciliation. No answer will do for him but the answer that God only can give; for who but God can justify God’s ways to his creature?

===Chinese===

但他确实否认自己曾是个恶人、行过他知道为恶之事：他确实否认自己里面有任何诡诈。而谁，因为知道自己并哀叹自己里面的诡诈，就敢否认世上曾有过一个拿但业（Nathanael）？约伯若是加尔文主义（Calvinist）者或路德宗者，《约伯记》就会很不一样。他的困惑就会是：神既是公义的，怎能要求人多于他所能行的，又刑罚他、仿佛他的罪是一位完全者明知其一切穷凶极恶仍选择去行的那罪。至于我，我不称任何人为主、唯独基督——从他我学到：他与我们的争执，在于我们不肯行我们所知的，不肯到他那里得生命。立足于人之所不肯、而非之所已行_的劝责，于人将有何等无尽更大的力量！
约伯孩子式的对神的判断，从未被任何低级理论的玷污所败坏歪曲——那些理论，唉！我们只能称之为流行的：它们对那位大父是羞辱；对那不认识*他*的人对神之道的解释，受那些不在乎认识他、满足于远远站着盯看那发出雷轰与声音之云的人欢迎；对那愿意起来到父那里去的人，却是威胁要把他们压沉到陀斐特的重担、难以担负的重担。约伯对神的公义（the justice of God）的观念与临到他之事之间的矛盾，不断缠绕他；它的刺远痛过一切别的折磨他的苦难；但它没有被一个比它自己更可怕的被接受的解释钉死在地狱的无望里。任世界斯芬克斯出多少谜，只要人等候那位世界救赎者的回答，它就吞不了任何人。约伯拒绝朋友们_的解释，因为他知道那是假的；他若接受了今日许多人会给他的那类解释，就是立刻被那怪物吞吃。他只是紧紧抓住神衣裳的繸子——围困他的门——一遍又一遍地重问，永远萦绕那唯一真回答与和好之源。唯有神能给的回答才能满足他；因为除了神，谁能向他的受造者称义神的道路？

===Original===

From a soul whose very consciousness is contradiction, we must not look for logic; misery is rarely logical; it is itself a discord; yet is it nothing less than natural that, *feeling* as if God wronged him, Job should yet be ever yearning after a sight of God, straining into his presence, longing to stand face to face with him. He would confront the One. He is convinced, or at least cherishes as his one hope the idea, that, if he could but get God to listen to him, if he might but lay his case clear before him, God would not fail to see how the thing was, and would explain the matter to him﻿—would certainly give him peace; the man in the ashes would know that the foundations of the world yet stand sure; that God has not closed his eyes, or﻿—horror of all horrors﻿—ceased to be just! Therefore would he order his words before him, and hear what God had to say; surely the Just would set the mind of his justice-loving creature at rest!
His friends, good men, religious men, but of the pharisaic type﻿—that is, men who would pay their court to God, instead of coming into his presence as children; men with traditional theories which have served their poor turn, satisfied their feeble intellectual demands, they think others therefore must accept or perish; men anxious to appease God rather than trust in him; men who would rather receive salvation from God, than God their salvation﻿—these his friends would persuade Job to the confession that he was a hypocrite, insisting that such things could not have come upon him but because of wickedness, and as they knew of none open, it must be for some secret vileness. They grow angry with him when he refuses to be persuaded against his knowledge of himself. They insist on his hypocrisy, he on his righteousness. Nor may we forget that herein lies not any overweening on the part of Job, for the poem prepares us for the right understanding of the man by telling us in the prologue, that God said thus to the accuser of men: “Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil?” God gives Job into Satan’s hand with confidence in the result; and at the end of the trial approves of what Job has said concerning himself.

===Chinese===

从_一个意识本身即矛盾的灵魂，我们不可指望逻辑；苦难很少有逻辑；它自身就是不和谐；然而，约伯*感觉*仿佛神亏负了他，却仍一直渴慕一见神、竭力挤进他面前、渴望与他面对面，这再自然不过。他要直面那一位。他确信、或至少怀抱为他唯一盼望的是：只要能让神听他，只要能把案情向他摆明，神必不会看不出事情的原委，必向他解释这事——必赐他平安；灰中的那人将知道世界的根基仍立得稳；神没有闭上眼，也没有——恐怖中的恐怖——不再是公义的！所以他要在他面前陈明他的话，听神有什么说；那公义者 Surely 必使他这爱公义之受造者的心得安息！
他的朋友们——好人、宗教徒，却属法利赛类型——就是那种向神进贡朝拜、而不像孩子那样进到他面前的人；持着为他们那可怜的一时效过力、满足过他们微弱智性要求的传统理论、以为别人就必须接受或灭亡的人；急于安抚神过于信靠神的人；宁愿从神领受救恩、而不愿领受神作他们救恩的人——这些朋友要劝约伯认罪、承认自己是伪君子，坚称这样的事临到他必是因为恶行，既然没有公开的恶行可见，就必是某种隐秘的卑劣。他们见他拒绝被说服违背对自己的认识，就向他发怒。他们坚执他的伪善，他坚执自己的义。我们也不可忘记这_里并无约伯的自负，因为诗在序言里就告诉我们、预备我们正确认识这个人：神对那控告人者这样说：“你曾用心察看我的仆人约伯没有？地上再没有人像他完全正直、敬畏神、远离恶事。”神把约伯交在撒但手里，对结果满怀信心；试炼的末了又称许约伯关于自己所说的话。

===Original===

But the very appearance of God is enough to make Job turn against himself: his part was to have trusted God altogether, in spite of every appearance, in spite of every reality! He will justify himself no more. He sees that though God has not been punishing him for his sins, yet is he far from what he ought to be, and must become: “Behold,” he says, “I am vile; what shall I answer thee? I will lay mine hand upon my mouth.”
But let us look a little closer at Job’s way of thinking and speaking about God, and his manner of addressing him﻿—so different from the pharisaic in all ages, in none more than in our own.
Waxing indignant at the idea that his nature required such treatment﻿—“Am I a sea or a whale,” he cries out, “that thou settest a watch over me?” *Thou knowest that I am not wicked*. “Thou settest a print upon the heels of my feet!”﻿—*that the way I have gone may be known by my footprints!* To his friends he cries: “Will ye speak wickedly for God? and talk deceitfully for him?” *Do you not know that I am the man I say?* “Will ye accept His person?”﻿—*siding with Him against me?* “Will ye contend for God?”﻿—*be special pleaders for him, his partisans*? “Is it good that He should search you out? or as one man mocketh another, do ye so mock Him?”﻿—*saying what you do not think*? “He will surely reprove you, if ye do secretly accept persons!”﻿—*even the person of God himself*!
Such words are pleasing in the ear of the father of spirits. He is not a God to accept the flattery which declares him above obligation to his creatures; a God to demand of them a righteousness different from his own; a God to deal ungenerously with his poverty-stricken children; a God to make severest demands upon his little ones! Job is confident of receiving justice. There is a strange but most natural conflict of feeling in him. His faith is in truth profound, yet is he always complaining. It is but the form his faith takes in his trouble. Even while he declares the hardness and unfitness of the usage he is receiving, he yet seems assured that, to get things set right, all he needs is admission to the presence of God﻿—an interview with the Most High. To be heard must be to have justice.

===Chinese===

但神的显现本身已足以叫约伯转而反对自己：他的本分原是完全信靠神——不顾一切外观、不顾一切现实！他不再自称为义。他看见：神虽没有因他的罪刑罚他，他却远不是他该是、且必须成为的样子：“看哪，”他说，“我是卑贱的，我用什么回答你呢？只好用手捂口。”
但让我们更细看约伯思想并谈论神的方式、以及他对神的称呼方式——与历代的法利赛式如此不同，尤其与我们这时代。
他为自己的天性竟需要这样的对待而愤然——“我岂是洋海、岂是大鱼，”他喊道，“你竟防守我？”*你知道我并非恶人*。“你察验我脚后的足迹！”——*好叫我走过的路由我的脚印知晓*！他对朋友们喊：“你们要为神说不义的话吗？为他传诡诈的言语吗？”*你们岂不知道我就是我所说的人吗？*“你们要看情面吗？”——*偏袒他来对付我*？“你们要为神争论吗？”——*作他的辩护人、他的党羽*？“他查出你们来，这岂是好么？还是像人欺哄人一样，你们欺哄他吗？”——*说你们所不以为然的话*？“你们若暗中徇情面，他必要责备你们！”——*哪怕徇的是神自己的情面*！
这样的话在众灵之父耳中可悦。他不是一位接受“宣告他超然于对受造者义务”之谄媚的神；不是一位向他们要求一种异于他自己之义的神；不是一位以不厚道待他贫乏儿女的神；不是一位向他的小孩子们提出最严厉要求的神！约伯确信必得公义。他里面有一场奇特却极自然的情感冲突。他的信心实在深刻，却总在抱怨。那不过是他的信心在患难中所取的形式。他虽宣称自己所受待遇的严苛与不当，却似乎仍确信：要把事情摆正，他所需的一切只是被引到神面前——与至高者一晤。蒙垂听必即得公义。

===Original===

He uses language which, used by any living man, would horrify the religious of the present day, in proportion to the lack of truth in them, just as it horrified his three friends, the honest pharisees of the time, whose religion was “doctrine” and rebuke. God speaks not a word of rebuke to Job for the freedom of his speech:﻿—he has always been seeking such as Job to worship him. It is those who know only and respect the outsides of religion, such as never speak or think of God but as the *Almighty* or *Providence*, who will say of the man who would go close up to God, and speak to him out of the deepest in the nature he has made, “he is irreverent.” To utter the name of God in the drama﻿—highest of human arts, is with such men blasphemy. They pay court to God, not love him; they treat him as one far away, not as the one whose bosom is the only home. They accept God’s person. “Shall not his excellency”﻿—another thing quite than that you admire﻿—“make you afraid? Shall not his dread”﻿—another thing quite than that to which you show your pagan respect﻿—“fall upon you?”
In the desolation of this man, the truth of God seems to him, yet more plainly than hitherto, the one thing that holds together the world which by the word of his mouth came first into being. If God be not accessible, nothing but despair and hell are left the man so lately the greatest in the east. Like a child escaping from the dogs of the street, he flings the door to the wall, and rushes, nor looks behind him, to seek the presence of the living one. Bearing with him the burden of his death, he cries, “Look what thou hast laid upon me! Shall mortal man, the helpless creature thou hast made, bear cross like this?” He would cast his load at the feet of his maker!﻿—God is the God of comfort, known of man as the refuge, the life-giver, or not known at all. But alas! he cannot come to him! Nowhere can he see his face! He has hid himself from him! “Oh that I knew where I might find him! that I might come even to his seat! I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments. I would know the words which he would answer me, and understand what he would say unto me. Will he plead against me with his great power? No! but he would put strength in me. There the righteous might dispute with him; so should I be delivered forever from my judge.

===Chinese===

他所用的言语——若出自任何活着的人之口，会按今世宗教人士之缺乏真实的程度使他们惊骇，正如它惊骇了他那三位朋友、当时代诚实的法利赛人，他们的宗教就是“教义”与责备。神对约伯言语的自由没有一句责备：——他一直在寻找像约伯这样的人来敬拜他。那些只认识、只尊重宗教外表的人——那些从不以别的、只以*全能者*或*天意*谈及或想到神的人——才会论那要就近神、从他造的天性最深处向他说话的人说：“他不虔敬。”在戏剧——人类最高的艺术——里说出神的名，在这样的人看是亵渎。他们向神进贡，不爱他；他们待他如远方的一位，而不当作那胸怀是唯一家园的一位。他们看神的情面。“他的尊严”——完全不同于你所钦佩的那种东西——“岂不叫你们惧怕吗？他的可畏”——完全不同于你向之表异教敬意的那种东西——“岂不落在你身上吗？”
在这人的荒凉中，神的真理在他看来——比从前更清楚——是那使世界聚拢为一的唯一之物，世界本是借他口中的话首先存有的。神若不可就近，那么这不久前还是东方至大之人，就只剩下绝望与地狱。像一个逃离街上恶犬的孩子，他把门撞到墙上，头也不回地冲进去，寻求那存活者的面前。带着他死亡的重担，他喊：“看你加在我身上的！必死的人、你所造的无助之物，岂能担这样的十架？”他要把他的重担摔在造他者的脚前！——神是安慰的神，人认识他、以他为避难所、赐生命者，否则就全不认识。但唉！他不能到他那里去！处处看不见他的面！他向自己隐藏了！“惟愿我知道在哪里可以寻见神，能到他的台前！我就在他面前将我的案件陈明，满口辩白。我必知道他回答我的言语，明白他向我所说的话。他岂用大能与我争辩吗？必不这样！他必理会我。在他那里，正直人可以与他辩论；这样，我必永远脱离那审判我的。

===Original===

Behold, I go forward, but he is not there; and backward, but I cannot perceive him: on the left hand, where he doth work, but I cannot behold him: he hideth himself on the right hand, that I cannot see him: but he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold.”
He cannot find him! Yet is he in his presence all the time, and his words enter into the ear of God his Saviour.
The grandeur of the poem is that Job pleads his cause with God against all the remonstrance of religious authority, recognizing no one but God, and justified therein. And the grandest of all is this, that he implies, if he does not actually say, that God *owes* something to his creature. This is the beginning of the greatest discovery of all﻿—that God owes *himself* to the creature he has made in his image, for so he has made him incapable of living without him. This, his creatures’ highest claim upon him, is his divinest gift to them. For the fulfilling of this their claim he has sent his son, that he may himself, the father of him and of us, follow into our hearts. Perhaps the worst thing in a theology constructed out of man’s dull *possible*, and not out of the being and deeds and words of Jesus Christ, is the impression it conveys throughout that God acknowledges no such obligation. Are not we the clay, and he the potter? how can the clay claim from the potter? We are the clay, it is true, but *his* clay, but spiritual clay, live clay, with needs and desires﻿—and *rights*; we are clay, but clay worth the Son of God’s dying for, that it might learn to consent to be shaped unto honour. We can have no merits﻿—a *merit* is a thing impossible; but God has given us rights. Out of him we have nothing; but, created by him, come forth from him, we have even rights towards him﻿—ah, never, never *against* him! his whole desire and labour is to make us capable of claiming, and induce us to claim of him the things whose rights he bestowed in creating us. No claim had we to be created: that involves an absurdity; but, being made, we have claims on him who made us: our needs are our claims. A man who will not provide for the hunger of his child, is condemned by the whole world.
“Ah, but,” says the partisan of God, “the Almighty stands in a relation very different from that of an earthly father: there is no parallel.” I grant it: there is no parallel.

===Chinese===

看哪，我往前走，他不在那里；往后退，也不能见他；他在左边行事，我却不能看见；在右边隐藏，我也不能见他；然而他知道我所行的路；他试炼我之后，我必如精金显出。”
他找不到他！然而他始终在他面前，他的话进入神——他救主——的耳中。
这诗的宏伟在于：约伯不顾一切宗教权威的劝阻、唯认神而为自己与神辩，并且在这点上被称为义。而其中最宏伟的是：他暗示——若非明说——神对他的受造者*欠*着什么。这是一切最伟大发现的开端——神对他照自己形象所造的受造者，欠*他自己*；因为这样造了他，就使他没有神便不能活。这受造者对他至高的主张，正是他给他们的最属神的礼物。为成全这主张，他差了他的儿子，好叫他自己——他父、也是我们父的父——得以跟进我们的心。一种出自人迟钝之*可能*、而非出自耶稣基督的存有、作为与言语的神学，其最坏处也许就是通篇给出的印象：神不承认这样的义务。我们岂不是泥、他岂不是窑匠吗？泥怎能向窑匠主张？我们是泥，真的，但是*他的*泥、属灵的泥、活的泥，有需要、有愿望——且有*权利*；我们是泥，却是值得神的儿子为之死、好叫它学会同意被塑造成为尊贵的泥。我们不能有功德——*功德*是不可能的事；但神给了我们权利。出于他我们一无所有；但既被他创造、从他出来，我们对神也有权利——啊，决不是、决不是*敌对他*的权利！他全部的愿望与劳作，正是要使我们能主张、并促使我们向他主张那些他在创造我们时赋予其权利的东西。我们没有被造的权利：那包含荒谬；但既被造，我们就有权向那造我们的主张：我们的需要就是我们的权利。一个不给他孩子饥饿供食的父亲，为全世界所定罪。
“啊，可是，”那替神偏袒的人说，“全能者所处的关系与地上的父亲大不相同：没有类比。”我承认：没有类比。

===Original===

The man did not create the child, he only yielded to an impulse created in himself: God is infinitely more bound to provide for *his* child than any man is to provide for his. The relation is infinitely, divinely closer. It is God to whom every hunger, every aspiration, every desire, every longing of our nature is to be referred; he made all our needs﻿—made us the creatures of a thousand necessities﻿—and have we no claim on him? Nay, we have claims innumerable, infinite; and his one great claim on us is that we should claim our claims of him.
It is terrible to represent God as unrelated to us in the way of appeal to his righteousness. How should he be righteous without owing us anything? How would there be any right for the judge of all the earth to do if he owed nothing? Verily he owes us nothing that he does not pay like a God; but it is of the devil to imagine imperfection and disgrace in obligation. So far is God from thinking so that in every act of his being he lays himself under obligation to his creatures. Oh, the grandeur of his goodness, and righteousness, and fearless unselfishness! When doubt and dread invade, and the voice of love in the soul is dumb, what can please the father of men better than to hear his child cry to him from whom he came, “Here I am, O God! Thou hast made me: give me that which thou hast made me needing.” The child’s necessity, his weakness, his helplessness, are the strongest of all his claims. If I am a whale, I can claim a sea; if I am a sea, I claim room to roll, and break in waves after my kind; if I am a lion, I seek my meat from God; am I a child, this, beyond all other claims, I claim﻿—that, if any of my needs are denied me, it shall be by the love of a father, who will let me see his face, and allow me to plead my cause before him. And this must be just what God desires! What would he have, but that his children should claim their father? To what end are all his dealings with them, all his sufferings with and for and in them, but that they should claim their birthright? Is not their birthright what he made them for, made in them when he made them? Is it not what he has been putting forth his energy to give them ever since first he began them to be﻿—the divine nature, God himself? The child has, and must have, a claim on the father, a claim which it is the joy of the father’s heart to acknowledge.

===Chinese===

人并没有创造孩子，他只是屈服于自己里面被造的一个冲动：神供应*他的*孩子的义务，无限大于任何人供应自己孩子的义务。这关系无限地、属神地更亲。我们天性中每一个饥饿、每一次升腾、每一个愿望、每一份切慕，都当指向神；是他造了我们一切的需要——把我们造为千般必需的受造者——我们对神就没有主张吗？不，我们有无数、无限的主张；而他对我们唯一的大主张，就是我们要向他主张我们的主张。
把神描绘成在向他的义呼吁上与我们无关，是可怕的。他若不欠我们什么，怎么是公义的呢？全地的审判者若什么也不欠，还有什么正当可行呢？真的，凡他不欠的，他无一不像神一样偿付；但以为义务中有不完全与耻辱，是属魔鬼的。神远非这样想，以致他在他存有的每一个行动里，把自己放在对受造者的义务之下。哦，他的良善、公义（the justice of God）、与无畏的无私，何等宏伟！当疑惑与惊惧侵入、灵魂里爱的声音喑哑时，还有什么比听见他的孩子向他所从出的那位呼喊更讨人类之父喜悦——“神啊，我在这里！你造了我：请把你造我使我需要的那样东西给我。”孩子的必需、他的软弱、他的无助，是他一切主张中最强的。我若是一头鲸，我能主张一片海；我若是一片海，我主张翻滚的余地、照我的类起浪的自由；我若是一头狮子，我向神寻我的食物；我若是孩子，那么超过一切别的，我主张——我任何的需要若被拒，必须是被一位父的爱所拒，他要让我看见他的脸，容我在他面前陈情。而这必正是神所愿的！他要的是什么，岂不就是他的孩子们主张他们的父？他待他们的一切、与他们同受并为他们并在他们里面受的一切苦，为的岂不就是他们主张他们的长子名分？他们的长子名分岂不正是他造他们所为的、造他们时造在他们里面的？岂不正是他从起始他们以来一直倾力要给他们的——神性、神自己？孩子对父亲有、且必有一个主张，一个父亲的心以承认它为乐的主张。

===Original===

A created need is a created claim. God is the origin of both need and supply, the father of our necessities, the abundant giver of the good things. Right gloriously he meets the claims of his child! The story of Jesus is the heart of his answer, not primarily to the prayers, but to the divine necessities of the children he has sent out into his universe.
Away with the thought that God could have been a perfect, an adorable creator, doing anything less than he has done for his children! that any other kind of being than Jesus Christ could have been worthy of all-glorifying worship! that his nature demanded less of him than he has done! that his nature is not absolute love, absolute self-devotion﻿—could have been without these highest splendours!
In the light of this truth, let us then look at the words at the head of this sermon: “Oh that thou wouldest hide me in the grave!” Job appeals to his creator, whom his sufferings compel him to regard as displeased with him, though he knows not why. *We* know he was not displeased but Job had not read the preface to his own story. He prays him to hide him, and forget him for a time, that the desire of the maker to look again upon the creature he had made, to see once more the work of his hands, may awake within him; that silence and absence and loss may speak for the buried one, and make the heart of the parent remember and long after the face of the child; then “thou shalt call and I will answer thee: thou wilt have a desire to the work of thine hands”; then will he rise in joy, to plead with confidence the cause of his righteousness. For God is nigher to the man than is anything God has made: what can be closer than the making and the made? that which is, and that which is because the other is? that which wills, and that which answers, owing to the will, the heart, the desire of the other, its power to answer? What other relation imaginable could give claims to compare with those arising from such a relation? God must love his creature that looks up to him with hungry eyes﻿—hungry for life, for acknowledgment, for justice, for the possibilities of living that life which the making life has made him alive for the sake of living.

===Chinese===

被造的需要就是被造的主张。神是需要与供应两边的本源、我们诸必需之父、美物之丰盛的赐予者。他何等荣耀地应付他孩子的主张！耶稣的故事是他回答的心脏——首要的不是对祷告（prayer）的回答，而是对他差进他宇宙中之儿女们属神必需的回答。
除去这想法：神本可以作一个完全的、可敬拜的创造者，却为他孩子们作的少于他已作的！除去这想法：除了耶稣基督那样的存有，还有别的什么配得全然荣耀的敬拜！除去这想法：他的本性对他的要求少于他已作的！除去这想法：他的本性不是绝对的爱、绝对的舍己——竟能没有这些最高的光辉！
在这真理的光中，让我们看本讲开头的话：“惟愿你把我藏在阴间！”约伯向他创造者呼吁，他的苦难迫使他看那创造者对他不悦，虽然他不知为何。*我们*知道他并非不悦，但约伯没有读过他自己故事的序言。他求他把他藏起来、暂时忘记他，好叫那造者要再看他所造之受造物、要再看他手之工的愿望，在他里面苏醒；好叫静默与缺席与失落为那埋葬者说话，使为父的心记起并切慕孩子的脸；那时“你呼叫，我便回答；你手所做的，你必渴望”；那时他必欢然起来，凭他义的自信陈情。因为神比他所造的任何东西都更近于人：还有什么比那造与被造更亲？那存有的、与那因另一者存有而存有的？那意愿的、与那回应的——它应答的能力系于另一者的意志、心与愿望？还有什么别的关系，能生出可与这关系所生之主张相比的主张？神必爱那以饥饿的眼仰望他的受造者——饿慕生命、饿慕承认、饿慕公义、饿慕活出那为活而使他活的生命之诸般可能。

===Original===

The whole existence of a creature is a unit, an entirety of claim upon his creator:﻿—just *therefore*, let him do with me as he will﻿—even to seating me in the ashes, and seeing me scrape myself with a potsherd!﻿—not the less but ever the more will I bring forward my claim! assert it﻿—insist on it﻿—assail with it the ear and the heart of the father. Is it not the sweetest music ear of maker can hear?﻿—except the word of perfect son, “Lo, I come to do thy will, O God!” We, imperfect sons, shall learn to say the same words too: that we may grow capable and say them, and so enter into our birthright, yea, become partakers of the divine nature in its divinest element, that Son came to us﻿—died for the slaying of our selfishness, the destruction of our mean hollow pride, the waking of our childhood. We are his father’s debtors for our needs, our rights, our claims, and he will have us pay the uttermost farthing. Yes, so true is the Father, he will even compel us, through misery if needful, to put in our claims, for he knows we have eternal need of these things: without the essential rights of his being, who can live?
I protest, therefore, against all such teaching as, originating in and fostered by the faithlessness of the human heart, gives the impression that the exceeding goodness of God towards man is not the natural and necessary outcome of his being. The root of every heresy popular in the church draws its nourishment merely and only from the soil of unbelief. The idea that God would be God all the same, as glorious as he needed to be, had he not taken upon himself the divine toil of bringing home his wandered children, had he done nothing to seek and save the lost, is false as hell. Lying for God could go no farther. As if the idea of God admitted of his being less than he is, less than perfect, less than all-in-all, less than Jesus Christ! less than Love absolute, less than entire unselfishness! As if the God revealed to us in the New Testament were not his own perfect necessity of loving-kindness, but one who has made himself better than, by his own nature, by his own love, by the laws which he willed the laws of his existence, he needed to be! They would have it that, being unbound, he deserves the greater homage! So it might be, if he were not our father.

===Chinese===

受造者的整个存在是一个单元、一个对神主张的总体：——正*因此*，随他怎样待我——哪怕叫我坐在炉灰中、看我拿瓦片刮自己！——不但不减、反倒越发我要提出我的主张！申明它——坚持它——用它敲击父的耳与心。这岂不是造者之耳能听的最甜美音乐？——除了那完全之子的话：“神啊，我来了，为要照你的旨意行！”我们这些不完全的儿子也必学会说同样的话：为叫我们能长大到会说、从而进入我们的长子名分、是的、在神性那最属神的元素上有分，那子来到我们中间——为杀死我们的自私、毁掉我们卑劣空洞的骄傲、唤醒我们的童年而死。我们因我们的需要、我们的权利、我们的主张，欠那位父的债，而他要我们还清最后一文钱。是的，父如此真实，他甚至要强迫我们——若必要、借苦难——提出我们的主张，因为他知道我们对这些有永远的需要：没有他存有之本质的权利，谁能活呢？
因此我抗议一切这样的教导——它出于人心之不信、也受其滋养——它给人的印象是：神对人的极高良善，不是他存有自然而又必然的结果。教会流行的每一个异端，其根都单单从不信之土里汲取养分。那种以为神若不曾担起把流浪儿女带回家的神圣劳苦、若没有去寻找拯救失丧者，也照样是神、也照样有他所需要的那样荣耀的观念，是地狱般的虚假。为神说谎无过于此。仿佛神的观念容许他少于他所是的、少于完全、少于在一切之中作一切、少于耶稣基督！少于绝对的爱、少于全然的舍己！仿佛新约向我们启示的神不是他自己慈爱的完全必需，而是一位把自己弄得好过他照自己的本性、自己的爱、他定为存在之律的诸律所需要是的！他们要我们以为：他既不受约束，就更配得敬拜！若他不是我们的父，或许如此。

===Original===

But to think of the living God not as our father, but as one who has condescended greatly, being nowise, in his own willed grandeur of righteous nature, bound to do as he has done, is killing to all but a slavish devotion. It is to think of him as nothing like the God we see in Jesus Christ.
It will be answered that we have fallen, and God is thereby freed from any obligation, if any ever were. It is but another lie. No amount of wrongdoing in a child can ever free a parent from the divine necessity of doing all he can to deliver his child; the bond between them cannot be broken. It is the vulgar, slavish, worldly idea of freedom, that it consists in being bound to nothing. Not such is God’s idea of liberty! To speak as a man﻿—the more of vital obligation he lays on himself, the more children he creates, with the more claims upon him, the freer is he as creator and giver of life, which is the essence of his Godhead: to make scope for his essence is to be free. Our Lord teaches us that the truth, known by obedience to him, will make us free: our freedom lies in living the truth of our relations to God and man. For a man to be alone in the universe would be to be a slave to unspeakable longings and lonelinesses. And again to speak after the manner of men: God could not be satisfied with himself without doing all that a God and Father could do for the creatures he had made﻿—that is, without doing just what he has done, what he is doing, what he will do, to deliver his sons and daughters, and bring them home with rejoicing. To answer the cry of the human heart, “Would that I could see him! would that I might come before him, and look upon him face to face!” he sent his son, the express image of his person. And again, that we might not be limited in our understanding of God by the constant presence to our weak and dullable spiritual sense of any embodiment whatever, he took him away. Having seen him, in his absence we understand him better. That we might know him he came; that we might go to him he went.

===Chinese===

但把活神不作我们的父、而想成一位大大屈尊者——在他自己公义性情的自愿宏伟中原无义务像他已作的那样行——这对一切非奴性的虔诚都是杀害。那是把他想得全然不像我们在耶稣基督里所见的那位神。
会有人回答：我们堕落了，神因此从一切义务中得了释放——若曾有过什么义务。那又是一个谎。孩子无论行多少错，都永远不能使父母脱离尽其所能搭救孩子的神圣必需；他们之间的纽带不能断。以为自由就在于不受任何约束，那是庸俗的、奴性的、属世的观念。神的自由观念不是这样！照人的说法——他加给自己的重大义务越多、他造的孩子越多、对他的主张越多，他作为创造者与生命赐予者就越自由，而那正是他神格的本质：为自己的本质开出空间，就是自由。我们主教导我们：借顺服（obedience）他而认识的真理必叫我们自由：我们的自由在于活出我们与神与人关系的真理。一个人在宇宙中独自存在，就是作说不出的切慕与孤独的奴仆。再照人的说法：神若不为他所造的受造者作一位神与父所能作的一切——就是说，不作他已作的、正在作的、将要作的、来拯救他儿女并欢然带他们回家的一切，他就不能对自己满足。为回答人心的呼喊“巴不得我能见他！巴不得我能到他面前、面对面看他！”他差了他的儿子、他本体的真像。又为叫我们对神的认识、不因任何具体形象总在我们软弱易钝的属灵感官面前、而受限制，他把他接去了。见过他之后，在他的不在中我们更明白他。为叫我们认识他，他来了；为叫我们归向他，他去了。

===Original===

If we dare, like Job, to plead with him in any of the heart-eating troubles that arise from the impossibility of loving such misrepresentation of him as is held out to us to love by our would-be teachers; if we think and speak out before him that which seems to us to be right, will he not be heartily pleased with his children’s love of righteousness﻿—with the truth that will not part him and his righteousness? Verily he will not plead against us with his great power, but will put strength in us, and where we are wrong will instruct us. For the heart that wants to do and think aright, the heart that seeks to worship him as no tyrant, but as the perfectly, absolutely righteous God, is the delight of the Father. To the heart that will not call that righteousness which it feels to be unjust, but clings to the skirt of his garment, and lifts pleading eyes to his countenance﻿—to that heart he will lay open the riches of his being﻿—riches which it has not entered that heart to conceive. “O Lord, they tell me I have so offended against thy law that, as I am, thou canst not look upon me, but threatenest me with eternal banishment from thy presence. But if thou look not upon me, how can I ever be other than I am? Lord, remember I was born in sin: how then can I see sin as thou seest it? Remember, Lord, that I have never known myself clean: how can I cleanse myself? Thou must needs take me as I am and cleanse me. Is it not impossible that I should behold the final goodness of good, the final evilness of evil? how then can I deserve eternal torment? Had I known good and evil, seeing them as thou seest them, then chosen the evil, and turned away from the good, I know not what I should not deserve; but thou knowest it has ever been something good in the evil that has enticed my selfish heart﻿—nor mine only, but that of all my kind. Thou requirest of us to forgive: surely thou forgivest freely! Bound thou mayest be to destroy evil, but art thou bound to keep the sinner alive that thou mayest punish him, even if it make him no better? Sin cannot be deep as life, for thou art the life; and sorrow and pain go deeper than sin, for they reach to the divine in us: thou canst suffer, though thou wilt not sin. To see men suffer might make us shun evil, but it never could make us hate it.

===Chinese===

我们若敢像约伯那样，在一切因“不可能爱那自命教师们摆给我们叫我们爱的、对他那样的歪曲”而噬心的烦恼中与他辩诉；我们若在他面前想我们所认为正当的、说我们所认为正当的，他岂不衷心喜悦他儿女对义的爱——喜悦那不肯把他与他的义分开的真理？他实在必不用大能与我们争辩，必把力量放在我们里面，我们错的地方必指教我们。因为那要行对思对的心、那要敬拜他非如暴君、而是如完全绝对公义之神的心，是父的喜乐。对那不肯把它感觉为不义的称为义、而抓住他衣裳的繸子、举恳求的眼望他脸的心——对那颗心，他必敞开他存有的丰盛——那心从未设想过的丰盛。“主啊，他们告诉我，我得罪你的律太深，以致照我现在这样，你不能看我，只以从你面前永远放逐来威吓我。但你若不看我，我怎能变得与现在不同？主啊，记念我是生在罪中的：我怎能像你看罪那样看罪？记念，主啊，我从不知道自己是洁净的：我怎能洁净自己？你必须照我的本相接我、洁净我。我岂能看见善之终极的善、恶之终极的恶？那怎能配受永远的苦刑？我若曾知道善恶、像你那样看它们、然后择恶弃善，我不知道自己有什么不配受的；但你知道，一直引诱我自私之心的，总是恶里面的某种善——不止我的心，我全类的心都是。你要求我们饶恕：你确实白白地饶恕！你受约束要毁掉恶，但你岂受约束要叫罪人活着、好刑罚他、哪怕这不能叫他变好？罪不能深如生命，因为你是生命；而忧伤与痛苦比罪更深，因为它们达到我们里面的属神者：你能受苦，虽然你不愿犯罪。看人受苦能使我们避开恶，却永不能使我们恨恶它。

===Original===

We might see thereby that thou hatest sin, but we never could see that thou lovest the sinner. Chastise us, we pray thee, in loving kindness, and we shall not faint. We have done much that is evil, yea, evil is very deep in us, but we are not all evil, for we love righteousness; and art not thou thyself, in thy Son, the sacrifice for our sins, the atonement of out breach? Thou hast made us subject to vanity, but hast thyself taken thy godlike share of the consequences. Could we ever have come to know good as thou knowest it, save by passing through the sea of sin and the fire of cleansing? They tell me I must say ‘for Christ’s sake,’ or thou wilt not pardon: it takes the very heart out of my poor love to hear that thou wilt not pardon me except because Christ has loved me; but I give thee thanks that nowhere in the record of thy gospel, does one of thy servants say any such word. In spite of all our fears and grovelling, our weakness, and our wrongs, thou wilt be to us what thou art﻿—such a perfect Father as no most loving child-heart on earth could invent the thought of! Thou wilt take our sins on thyself, giving us thy life to live withal. Thou bearest our griefs and carriest our sorrows; and surely thou wilt one day enable us to pay every debt we owe to each other! Thou wilt be to us a right generous, abundant father! Then truly our hearts shall be jubilant, because thou art what thou art﻿—infinitely beyond all we could imagine. Thou wilt humble and raise us up. Thou hast given thyself to us that, having thee, we may be eternally alive with thy life. We run within the circle of what men call thy wrath, and find ourselves clasped in the zone of thy love!”
But be it well understood that when I say *rights*, I do not mean *merits*﻿—of any sort. We can deserve from him nothing at all, in the sense of any right proceeding from ourselves. All our rights are such as the bounty of love inconceivable has glorified our being with﻿—bestowed for the one only purpose of giving the satisfaction, the fulfilment of the same﻿—rights so deep, so high, so delicate, that their satisfaction cannot be given until we desire it﻿—yea long for it with our deepest desire.

===Chinese===

借那样我们或许能看见你恨恶罪，却永不能看见你爱罪人。求你在慈爱中管教我们，我们必不昏倒。我们行了许多恶，是的，恶在我们里面很深，但我们不全是恶，因为我们爱义（righteousness）；你自己、在你的儿子里，岂不就是为我们诸罪的祭、我们这破裂的赎罪（atonement）吗？你使我们服在虚空之下，却亲自担当了你属神的那份后果。若非经过罪之海与炼净之火，我们岂能像你那样认识善？他们告诉我必须说‘因基督的缘故’，否则你不肯赦免：听说你不肯赦免我、除非因为基督爱过我，这话把我那可怜的爱的心都掏空了；但我感谢你，在你福音的记载里，你的仆人没有一个说过这样的话。不顾我们一切的恐惧与卑屈、我们的软弱与我们的过犯，你必对我们作你所是的——那样一位完全的父，地上最慈爱的孩子心也发明不出对他的想望！你必把我们的罪担在你自己身上，把你的生命给我们靠着活。你担当我们的忧患、背负我们的痛苦；而你确有一日必使我们能还清我们彼此所欠的每一笔债！你必作我们正当慷慨、丰盛的父！那时我们的心真要欢呼，因为你是你所是的——无限超出我们所能想象。你必降卑我们又举起我们。你已把你自己给了我们，好叫我们有了你、便永远以你的生命而活。我们在人所谓的你的怒气之圈中奔跑，却发现自己在神爱的怀抱里！”
但要明白：当我说*权利*时，我不是指*功德*——任何意义上的。我们配不得从他来的任何东西——凡出于我们自己之义的意义上的。我们一切的权利，都是那不可思议之爱的厚赐用以荣耀我们存有的权利——赐下的唯一目的，是给它们以满足与成全——那权利如此深、如此高、如此精微，以至于在我们渴望它之前——是的、以我们最深的渴望切慕它之前——它们的满足不能给出。

===Original===

The giver of them came to men, lived with men, and died by the hands of men, that they might possess these rights abundantly: more not God could do to fulfil his part﻿—save indeed what he is doing still every hour, every moment, for every individual. Our rights are rights with God himself at the heart of them. He could recall them if he pleased, but only by recalling us, by making us cease. While we exist, by the being that is ours, they are ours. If he could not fulfil our rights to us﻿—because we would not have them, that is﻿—if he could not make us such as to care for these rights which he has given us out of the very depth of his creative being, I think he would have to uncreate us. But as to deserving, that is absurd: he had to die in the endeavour to make us listen and receive. “When ye shall have done all the things that are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants; we have done that which it was our duty to do.” Duty is a thing prepaid: it can never have desert. There is no claim on God that springs from us: all is from him.
But, lest it should be possible that any unchildlike soul might, in arrogance and ignorance, think to stand upon his rights *against* God, and demand of him this or that after the will of the flesh, I will lay before such a possible one some of the things to which he has a right, yea, perhaps has first of all a right to, from the God of his life, because of the beginning he has given him﻿—because of the divine germ that is in him. He has a claim on God, then, a divine claim, for any pain, want, disappointment, or misery, that would help to show him to himself as the fool he is; he has a claim to be punished to the last scorpion of the whip, to be spared not one pang that may urge him towards repentance; yea, he has a claim to be sent out into the outer darkness, whether what we call hell, or something speechlessly worse, if nothing less will do.

===Chinese===

那赐权者来到人中间、与人同住、死于人之手，好叫他们丰盛地拥有这些权利：为尽他的分，神不能作更多——除了他此刻每小时、每刻、为每个_人仍在作的。我们的权利是以神自己为其心的权利。他若愿意可以收回它们，但只能借收回我们、借使我们止息。我们一日存在，凭那属于我们的存有，它们就属于我们。他若不能向我们成全我们的权利——因为我们不肯要它们，就是说——他若不能把我们作成在乎这些权利的人、这些他从他自己创造存有之深处给我们的权利，我想他就不得不把我们取消。至于配得，那是荒谬：他不得不死在叫我们肯听肯受的努力中。“你们作完了一切所吩咐的，只当说：我们是无用的仆人；所作的本是我们应分作的。”本分是一件预付的事：它永远不能生功德。对神没有一样主张出于我们：一切都出于他。
但免得有某个不像孩子的灵魂、可能在傲慢与无知中想*敌对*神而立在他的权利上、照肉体的意志向他要求这那，我要把这一个人从他的生命之神那里、因他所给他的开端、因他里面的属神胚芽、有权得到的——是的、或许首先有权得到的——几样东西摆在他面前。他对神有一个主张，一个属神的主张：为任何能帮助把他这个愚人显给他自己的疼痛、贫乏、失望或苦难；他有权被鞭打到最后一只蝎子，不宽免任何一样能推他向悔改的痛苦；是的，若非如此不行，他有权被送到外边黑暗（the outer darkness）——无论那是我们所谓地狱（hell）、还是说不出地更坏的东西。

===Original===

He has a claim to be compelled to repent; to be hedged in on every side; to have one after another of the strong, sharp-toothed sheepdogs of the great shepherd sent after him, to thwart him in any desire, foil him in any plan, frustrate him of any hope, until he come to see at length that nothing will ease his pain, nothing make life a thing worth having, but the presence of the living God within him; that nothing is good but the will of God; nothing noble enough for the desire of the heart of man but oneness with the eternal. For this God must make him yield his very being, that He may enter in and dwell with him.
That the man would enforce none of these claims, is nothing; for it is not a man who owes them to him, but the eternal God, who by his own will of right towards the creature he has made, is bound to discharge them. God has to answer to himself for his idea; he has to do with the need of the nature he made, not with the self-born choice of the self-ruined man. His candle yet burns dim in the man’s soul; that candle must shine as the sun. For what is the all-pervading dissatisfaction of his wretched being but an unrecognized hunger after the righteousness of his father. The soul God made is thus hungering, though the selfish, usurping self, which is its consciousness, is hungering only after low and selfish things, ever trying, but in vain, to fill its mean, narrow content, with husks too poor for its poverty-stricken desires. For even that most degraded chamber of the soul which is the temple of the deified Self, cannot be filled with less than God; even the usurping Self must be miserable until it cease to look at itself in the mirror of Satan, and open the door of its innermost closet to the God who means to dwell there, and make peace.
He that has looked on the face of God in Jesus Christ, whose heart overflows, if ever so little, with answering love, sees God standing with full hands to give the abundance for which he created his children, and those children hanging back, refusing to take, doubting the God-heart which knows itself absolute in truth and love.
It is not at first easy to see wherein God gives Job any answer; I cannot find that he offers him the least explanation of why he has so afflicted him.

===Chinese===

他有权被强制悔改；被四面围困；有大牧人一只接一只那些强壮、利齿的牧羊犬被差来追他，挫败他任何的愿望、打破他任何的计划、落空他任何的盼望，直到他终于看见：没有什么能解他的痛，没有什么能使生命值得拥有，唯有那活神在他里面的同在；唯有神的旨意（the will of God）是善；没有什么配得上人心的愿望，唯有与永恒者为一。为这个，神必须使他交出他非常的存有，好叫他进来与他同住。
那人会不会去要求这些主张中的一项，无关紧要；因为欠他这些的不是人，而是那永恒的神，他凭自己对所造受造者的正当意志，受了约束要履行它们。神必须向他自己交代他的观念；他要对付的是他所造之天性的需要，不是那自我毁坏者自生的选择。他的烛在那人灵魂里仍烧得昏暗；那烛必须亮如太阳。因为他那悲惨存有中那弥漫的不满，岂不正是对他父之义的一场未被认出的饥饿。神所造的灵魂正这样饿着，虽然那自私、僭位的自我——灵魂的意识——只饿着低俗自私之物，总想、却总不能用它贫乏的欲望所嫌太粗的荚壳，填满它卑劣窄小的内容。因为连灵魂那最堕落的小室——那被神化之自我的殿——也不能以少于神的东西填满；连那僭位的自我也必悲惨，直到它不再从撒但的镜中看自己、把它最内之室的门向那定意住在其中、作平安的神打开。
凡在耶稣基督里见过神的脸、心里满溢着——哪怕一点点——回应之爱的人，都看见神满手站着、要赐他为他儿女所造的丰盛，而那些儿女却退缩着、不肯拿、怀疑着那自知在真理与爱中绝对的神心。
起初不容易看出神在哪里给了约伯回答；我找不到他给他一丝一毫为何如此苦待他的解释。

===Original===

He justifies him in his words; he says Job has spoken what is right concerning him, and his friends have not; and he calls up before him, one after another, the works of his hands. The answer, like some of our Lord’s answers if not all of them, seems addressed to Job himself, not to his intellect; to the revealing, Godlike imagination in the man, and to no logical faculty whatever. It consists in a setting forth of the power of God, as seen in his handywork, and wondered at by the men of the time; and all that is said concerning them has to do with their show of themselves to the eyes of men. In what belongs to the deeper meanings of nature and her mediation between us and God, the appearances of nature are the truths of nature, far deeper than any scientific discoveries in and concerning them. The show of things is that for which God cares *most*, for their show is the face of far deeper things than they; we see in them, in a distant way, as in a glass darkly, the face of the unseen. It is through their show, not through their analysis, that we enter into their deepest truths. What they say to the childlike soul is the truest thing to be gathered of them. To know a primrose is a higher thing than to know all the botany of it﻿—just as to know Christ is an infinitely higher thing than to know all theology, all that is said about his person, or babbled about his work. The body of man does not exist for the sake of its hidden secrets; its hidden secrets exist for the sake of its outside﻿—for the face and the form in which dwells revelation: its outside is the deepest of it. So Nature as well exists primarily for her face, her look, her appeals to the heart and the imagination, her simple service to human need, and not for the secrets to be discovered in her and turned to man’s farther use. What in the name of God is our knowledge of the elements of the atmosphere to our knowledge of the elements of Nature? What are its oxygen, its hydrogen, its nitrogen, its carbonic acid, its ozone, and all the possible rest, to the blowing of the wind on our faces? What is the analysis of water to the babble of a running stream? What is any knowledge of things to the heart, beside its child-play with the Eternal!

他在他的言语上称他为义；他说约伯论到他说得对、而他朋友们不对；他又把神手的作为一样接一样地唤到他面前。这回答，像我们主的一些回答（若非全部），似乎是向约伯本人、不是向他的悟性说的；向那人里面那启示性的、属神般的想象说的，而不是向任何逻辑官能。它在于陈说神的大能，如他手所作的、为当时代人所惊叹的；而所说关于那些工的一切，都关乎它们向人之眼的自我显示。在属于自然更深意义、及其在我们与神之间作中保的事上，自然的外观就是自然的真理，深过关于它们的任何科学发现。物的显示是神*最*看重的，因为它们的显示是远深于它们之物的面；我们借它们、以遥远的方式、如对着模糊的镜，看见那不可见者的面。是借它们的显示、不是借它们的分解，我们进入它们最深的真理。它们对童心所说的话，是从它们中间能收取的最真者。认识一朵樱草花，高于认识它全部的植物学——正如认识基督无限地高于认识全部神学、一切关于他位格的所说、关于他工作的空谈。人的身体不是为它隐藏的秘密而存在；它隐藏的秘密是为它的外面而存在——为那住着启示的脸与形——：它的外面是它最深的。自然也一样，首要为她的脸、她的神情、她向心与想象的诉求、她对人之需的单纯服事而存在，不为在她里面被发现、转为人的进一步用途的秘密。以神之名说，我们对大气成分的知识，与我们自己对自然诸元素的知识何干？它的氧、氢、氮、碳酸、臭氧，以及可能的一切其余，与我们脸上吹过的风何干？水的分析与溪流的潺潺何干？对心而言，任何对物的知识，与它和永恒者的孩童之戏相比算什么！

And by an infinite decomposition we should know nothing more of what a thing really is, for, the moment we decompose it, it ceases to be, and all its meaning is vanished. Infinitely more than astronomy even, which destroys nothing, can do for us, is done by the mere aspect and changes of the vault over our heads. Think for a moment what would be our idea of greatness, of God, of infinitude, of aspiration, if, instead of a blue, far withdrawn, light-spangled firmament, we were born and reared under a flat white ceiling! I would not be supposed to depreciate the labours of science, but I say its discoveries are unspeakably less precious than the merest gifts of Nature, those which, from morning to night, we take unthinking from her hands. One day, I trust, we shall be able to enter into their secrets from within them﻿—by natural contact between our heart and theirs. When we are one with God we may well understand in an hour things that no man of science, prosecuting his investigations from the surface with all the aids that keenest human intellect can supply, would reach in the longest lifetime. Whether such power will ever come to any man in this world, or can come only in some state of existence beyond it, matters nothing to me: the question does not interest me; life is one, and things will be then what they are now; for God is one and the same there and here; and I shall be the same there I am here, however larger the life with which it may please the Father of my being to endow me.
The argument implied, not expressed, in the poem, seems to be this﻿—that Job, seeing God so far before him in power, and his works so far beyond his understanding that they filled him with wonder and admiration﻿—the vast might of the creation, the times and the seasons, the marvels of the heavens, the springs of the sea, and the gates of death; the animals, their generations and providing, their beauties and instincts; the strange and awful beasts excelling the rest, behemoth on the land, leviathan in the sea, creatures, perhaps, now vanished from the living world;﻿—that Job, beholding these things, ought to have reasoned that he who could work so grandly beyond his understanding, must certainly use wisdom in things that touched him nearer, though they came no nearer his understanding: “shall he that contendeth with the Almighty instruct him?

而借无限的分解，我们并不会更多知道一物真正是什么；因为我们一分解它，它就不再是它，它全部的意义都消逝了。无限多过天文学——它什么也不毁坏——能为我们作的，是由我们头顶那穹苍单单的外观与变化作成的。想一刻：若我们生在、长在一片平白的天花板下、而非一片蓝色、辽远、缀光的穹苍下，我们对伟大、对神、对无限、对升腾的观念将是什么！我不要人以为我在贬低科学的劳作，但我宣告：它的发现说不出来地少于自然最微末的恩赐——那些我们从早到晚不经意从她手中领受的。有一日，我信，我们将能从其内、借我们的心与它们的心之间自然的接触，进入它们的秘密。当我们与神为一，我们或能在一小时内明白：那从表面着手、带着最锐利人类智性所能供的一切辅助进行调查的科学人、在最长的一生里也达不到。这样的能力是否会临到这世上的任何人，还是只能在未来某种存在状态中来临，于我无关紧要：这问题我不感兴趣；生命是一，事物到那时仍必如今日所是；因为神在那里在这里是同一位；我在那里也必是我在这里的这位，无论我存有的父乐意以多大的生命来装备我。

he that reproveth God, let him answer it.” “Wilt thou also disannul my judgment? wilt thou condemn me that thou mayest be righteous?” In this world power is no *proof* of righteousness; but was it likely that he who could create should be unrighteous? Did not all he made move the delight of the beholding man? Did such things foreshadow injustice towards the creature he had made in his image? If Job could not search his understanding in these things, why should he conclude his own case wrapt in the gloom of injustice? Did he understand his own being, history, and destiny? Should not God’s ways in these also be beyond his understanding? Might he not trust him to do him justice? In such high affairs as the rights of a live soul, might not matters be involved too high for Job? The maker of Job was so much greater than Job, that his ways with him might well be beyond his comprehension! God’s thoughts were higher than his thoughts, as the heavens were higher than the earth!
The true child, the righteous man, will trust absolutely, against all appearances, the God who has created in him the love of righteousness.
God does not, I say, tell Job why he had afflicted him: he rouses his child-heart to trust. All the rest of Job’s life on earth, I imagine, his slowly vanishing perplexities would yield him ever fresh meditations concerning God and his ways, new opportunities of trusting him, light upon many things concerning which he had not as yet begun to doubt, added means of growing in all directions into the knowledge of God. His perplexities would thus prove of divinest gift. Everything, in truth, which we cannot understand, is a closed book of larger knowledge and blessedness, whose clasps the blessed perplexity urges us to open. There is, there can be, nothing which is not in itself a righteous intelligibility﻿—whether an intelligibility for us, matters nothing. The awful thing would be, that anything should be in its nature unintelligible: that would be the same as *no God*. That God knows is enough for me; I shall know, if I can know. It would be death to think God did not know; it would be as much as to conclude there was no God to know.
How much more than Job are we bound, who know him in his Son as Love, to trust God in all the troubling questions that force themselves upon us concerning the motions and results of things!

那真实的孩子、那义人，必不顾一切外观，绝对信靠那在他里面造出爱义之神。
我说，神没有告诉约伯他为何苦待他：他唤起他的孩子之心去信靠。我想，约伯余生在地上，他那慢慢消散的困惑会不断给他对神与他的道路新的默想、新的信靠机会、照亮许多他尚未开始怀疑的事、增添他向各方生长进于神之认识的手段。他的困惑将因此证明是至属神的恩赐。实在说，凡我们不能明白的，都是一部更大知识与福乐的合着的书，那有福的困惑催促我们去打开它的扣。没有一样、也不可能有一样东西本身不是义的可解性——至于它对我们是否可解，无关紧要。可畏的倒是：任何东西在本性上不可解：那就等于*没有神*。神知道，于我就够；我若能知道，就必知道。想神不知道，就是死；那就等于断定没有知道的神。
我们既在他儿子身上认识他是爱，岂不比约伯更受约束、要在那些关于事物的运行与结局、强加于我们的一切搅扰之问题上信靠神！

With all those about the lower animals, with all those about such souls as seem never to wake from, or seem again to fall into the sleep of death, we will trust him.
In the confusion of Job’s thoughts﻿—how could they be other than confused, in the presence of the awful contradiction of two such facts staring each other in the face, that God was just, yet *punishing* a righteous man as if he were wicked?﻿—while he was not yet able to generate, or to receive the thought, that approving love itself might be inflicting or allowing the torture﻿—that such suffering as his was granted only to a righteous man, that he might be made perfect﻿—I can well imagine that at times, as the one moment he doubted God’s righteousness, and the next cried aloud, “Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him,” there must in the chaos have mingled some element of doubt as to the existence of God. Let not such doubt be supposed a yet further stage in unbelief. To deny the existence of God may, paradoxical as the statement will at first seem to some, involve less unbelief than the smallest yielding to doubt of his goodness. I say “yielding”; for a man may be haunted with doubts, and only grow thereby in faith. Doubts are the messengers of the Living One to rouse the honest. They are the first knock at our door of things that are not yet, but have to be, understood; and theirs in general is the inhospitable reception of angels that do not come in their own likeness. Doubt must precede every deeper assurance; for uncertainties are what we first see when we look into a region hitherto unknown, unexplored, unannexed. In all Job’s begging and longing to see God, then, may well be supposed to mingle the mighty desire to be assured of God’s being. To acknowledge is not to be sure of God. One great point in the poem is﻿—that when Job hears the voice of God, though it utters no word of explanation, it is enough to him to hear it: he knows that God is, and that he hears the cry of his creature. That he is there, knowing all about him, and what had befallen him, is enough; he needs no more to reconcile seeming contradictions, and the worst ills of outer life become endurable. Even if Job could not at first follow his argument of divine probability, God settled everything for him when, by answering him out of the whirlwind, he showed him that he had not forsaken him.

连同那些关于低等动物的、那些关于似乎从未从死睡中醒来、或似乎又落入死睡之灵魂的一切，我们要信靠他。
在约伯心思的混乱中——两个这样的事实当面相瞪：神是公义的，却*刑罚*一个义人如同他是恶人——他的心思怎能不混乱？——他还未能生出、或领受这思想：嘉许的爱本身可能正在施加或容许那折磨——这样的苦只赐给义人、好叫他得以完全——我可以想见，当他一刻疑惑神的义、下一刻又喊“他必杀我，我虽无指望、然而我还要信靠他”，那混沌里必掺着某种对神之存在的怀疑。不要以为这样的怀疑是不信的更深一级。否认神的存在——这话起初对某些人显得悖谬——所含的不信，可能少于对_他良善最小的一点让步。我说“让步”；因为人可能被疑惑纠缠，却反而因此信心增长。疑惑是那存活者的信差，来唤醒诚实的人。它们是那尚未存在、却必须被明白之事在我们门上的第一叩；它们的遭遇，一般说来，是不以本来形像而来的天使所受的冷遇。每一样更深的确据之前必有疑惑；因为不确定，正是我们望进一个迄今未知、未探、未并之境时首先看见的。所以在约伯一切求见神的恳求与切慕中，想必掺着要确知神存在的大愿望。承认不等于确知神。这诗的一大要点是——约伯听见神的声音时，虽然它没有吐出一个字的解释，听见就已足够：他知道神在，并且他听见他受造者的呼喊。他在那里、知道关于他与他所遭的一切，就够了；他不需要更多的来调和表面的矛盾，外面生活最坏的恶也变得可忍。即使约伯起初跟不上他那属神或然性的论证，当神从旋风中回答他、向他显明自己没有丢弃他时，神已为他解决了一切。

It is true that nothing but a far closer divine presence can ever make life a thing fit for a son of man﻿—and that for the simplest of all reasons, that he is made in the image of God, and it is for him absolutely imperative that he should have in him the reality of which his being is the image: while he has it not in him, his being, his conscious self, is but a mask, a spiritual emptiness; but for the present, Job, yielding to God, was calmed and satisfied. Perhaps he came at length to see that, if anything God could do to him would trouble him so as to make him doubt God﻿—if he knew him so imperfectly who could do nothing ill, then it was time that he should be so troubled, that the imperfection of his knowledge of God and his lack of faith in him should be revealed to him﻿—that an earthquake of his being should disclose its hollowness, and at the same time bring to the surface the gold of God that was in him. To know that our faith is weak is the first step towards its strengthening; to be capable of distrusting is death; to know that we are, and cry out, is to begin to live﻿—to begin to be made such that we cannot distrust﻿—such that God may do anything with us and we shall never doubt him. Until doubt is impossible, we are lacking in the true, the childlike knowledge of God; for either God is such that one *may* distrust him, or he is such that to distrust him is the greatest injustice of which a man can be guilty. If then we are able to distrust him, either we know God imperfect, or we do not know him. Perhaps Job learned something like this; anyhow, the result of what he had had to endure was a greater nearness to God. But all that he was required to receive at the moment was the argument from God’s loving wisdom in his power, to his loving wisdom in everything else. For power is a real and a good thing, giving an immediate impression that it proceeds from goodness. Nor, however long it may last after goodness is gone, was it ever born of anything but goodness. In a very deep sense, power and goodness are one. In the deepest fact they are one.
Seeing God, Job forgets all he wanted to say, all he thought he would say if he could but see him. The close of the poem is grandly abrupt.

诚然，唯有远更亲近的神圣同在，才能使生命配得上人子——理由再简单不过：他是照神的形象造的，他存有所像的那个实际、绝对必需在他里面；他没有它在他里面时，他的存有、他有意识的自己，不过是一副面具、一个属灵的空壳；但眼下，降服于神的约伯得了平静与满足。或许他至终看见：若神可能作的任何事会搅扰他到一个地步叫他疑惑神——若他这么不完全地认识那位不能行恶者——那正是他该这样被搅扰的时候，好叫他认识神的不完全与他信心的缺欠向他显明——好叫他存有的一场地震显出它的空，同时把在他里面神的那金子带到面上。知道我们信心软弱，是它得坚固的第一步；能不信是死；知道我们在、并呼喊，是开始活——开始被作成不能再不信的——被作成神无论怎样待我们、我们永不再疑惑他的。在疑惑成为不可能之前，我们缺少那真实的、孩子式的对神的认识；因为神要么是这样一位、人*可能*不信靠他的，要么是这样一位、不信靠他就是人所能犯的最大不义。我们若能不信靠他，或者我们认识神不完全，或者我们不认识他。或许约伯学到了类似这样的事；无论如何，他所必须忍受之事的结果，是与神更亲近。而他当时被要求领受的，只是从神能力中的慈爱智慧、推及万事中之慈爱智慧的论证。因为能力是一件真实而良善的东西，直接给出它出于良善的印象。而且无论良善逝去后它能存多久，它从来只生于良善。在极深的意义上，能力与良善是一。在最深的事实里它们是一。
约伯一看见神，就忘了他想说的一切、他想他若能见他就要说的一切。诗的结束宏伟而突兀。

I will lay mine hand upon my mouth. Once have I spoken; but I will not answer: yea, twice; but I will proceed no further.” Then again, after God has called to witness for him behemoth and leviathan, he replies, “I know that thou canst do everything, and that no thought can be withholden from thee. Who is he that hideth counsel without knowledge?” This question was the word with which first God made his presence known to him; and in the mouth of Job now repeating the question, it is the humble confession, “*I am that foolish man.*”﻿—“Therefore,” he goes on, “have I uttered that I understood not; things too wonderful for me, which I knew not.” He had not knowledge enough to have a right to speak. “Hear, I beseech thee, and I will speak:”﻿—In the time to come, he will yet cry﻿—to be taught, not to justify himself. “I will demand of thee, and declare thou unto me.”﻿—The more diligently yet will he seek to know the counsel of God. That he cannot understand will no longer distress him; it will only urge him to fresh endeavour after the knowledge of him who in all his doings is perfect. “I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee. Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes.”
Job had his desire: he saw the face of God﻿—and abhorred himself in dust and ashes. He sought justification; he found self-abhorrence. Was this punishment? The farthest from it possible. It was the best thing﻿—to begin with﻿—that the face of God could do for him. Blessedest gift is self-contempt, when the giver of it is the visible glory of the Living One.

===Chinese===

他原想在他面前陈明案情；他切望见他、好说话、为自己辩护，想象神同他那些义的朋友一样冤枉地控告他；但他的话没了；他一句话也说不出。在那位就是义者面前自称为义，在他看正如其本相——愚妄与无用的劳。神若不看他为义，他就不义，可以闭口了。他若义，神比他自己更清楚。不，神若不屑称他为义，约伯对自称为义也失了兴趣。他天性一切的恶与不完全，在那独一纯洁、独一正当、毫无自私者面前，都起来了。“看哪，”他喊，“我是卑贱的，我用什么回答你呢？只好用手捂口。一次我说话、不再答；是的、两次、我不再说。”然后，神又叫河马与鳄鱼为他作见证之后，他回答说：“我知道你万事都能作，你的旨意不能拦阻。谁用无知的言语使你的旨意隐藏呢？”这个问题正是神初次使他知道自己在场时所用的话；如今在约伯口中重复，它是谦卑的认罪：“*我就是那愚昧人*。”——“所以，”他接着说，“我所说的，是我不明白的；这些事太奇妙，是我不知道的。”他的知识不够、不够有说话的权利。“求你听我，我要说话”：——将来的时日，他仍要呼喊——为受教，不为自辩。“我要问你，求你指示我。”——他还必越发殷勤地寻求认识神的谋略。他所不能明白的，不再使他愁烦；它只催他重新努力去认识那位在他一切作为上都完全的神。如今约伯的心愿得了：他看见了神的脸——并且在尘土和炉灰中厌恶自己。他寻求称义；他寻见的是自我厌弃。这是刑罚吗？恰恰相反，再没有比这更远的了。这是神的脸所能为他作的——开头的——最好的事。自我轻视是最蒙福的恩赐，当赐下它的是那存活者可见的荣耀。

===Original===

For there to see is to partake; to be able to behold that glory is to live; to turn from and against self is to begin to be pure of heart. Job was in the right when he said that he did not deserve to be in such wise punished for his sins: neither did he deserve to see the face of God, yet had he that crown of all gifts given him﻿—and it was to see himself vile, and abhor himself. By very means of the sufferings against which he had cried out, the living one came near to him, and he was silent. Oh the divine generosity that will grant us to be abashed and self-condemned before the Holy!﻿—to come so nigh him as to see ourselves dark spots against his brightness! Verily we must be of his kind, else no show of him could make us feel small and ugly and unclean! Oh the love of the Father, that he should give us to compare ourselves with him, and be buried in humility and shame! To be rebuked before him is to be his. Good man as Job was, he had never yet been right near to God; now God has come near to him, has become very real to him; he knows now in very deed that God is he with whom he has to do. He had laid all these troubles upon him that He might through them draw nigh to him, and enable him to know him.
Two things are clearly contained in, and manifest from this poem:﻿—that not every man deserves for his sins to be punished everlastingly from the presence of the Lord; and that the best of men, when he sees the face of God, will know himself vile. God is just, and will never deal with the sinner as if he were capable of sinning the pure sin; yet if the best man be not delivered from himself, that self will sink him into Tophet.
Any man may, like Job, plead his cause with God﻿—though possibly it may not be to like justification: he gives us liberty to speak, and will hear with absolute fairness. But, blessed be God, the one result for all who so draw nigh to him will be﻿—to see him plainly, surely right, the perfect Saviour, the profoundest refuge even from the wrongs of their own being, yea, nearer to them always than any wrong they could commit; so seeing him, they will abhor themselves, and rejoice in him.

===Chinese===

因为在那里，看见就是有分；能观看那荣耀就是活；转离并抵挡自我，是心开始变纯。约伯说他不配为他_的罪受这样的刑罚，他说得对：他也不配见神的脸，然而他把那冠冕于一切礼物之上的给了他——那就是看见自己卑贱、并厌恶自己。正是借着他曾呼喊反对的那些苦难，那存活者临近了他，而他就静默了。哦，那容许我们在圣者面前羞愧自责的神圣宽宏！——临近他到看见自己是他光亮上的黑斑！真的，我们必是出于他的类，否则他的任何显示都不能使我们感觉渺小、丑陋、不洁！哦父的爱，他竟容我们把自己与他相比、被埋在谦卑与羞愧里！在他面前受责备，就是属于他。约伯虽是好人，却从未真正就近过神；如今神就近了他，对他成为非常真实；他如今实在知道：神就是他必须与之打交道的那位。他把这一切苦难加在他身上，正是要借它们就近他，使他得以认识他。
这诗清楚含着并显明两件事：——并非每个人都配为他的罪从主面前受永远的刑罚；而最好的人一看见神的脸，也必认识自己卑贱。神是公义的，永不会待罪人如同他能犯那纯全的罪；但最好的人若不蒙拯救脱离自我，那自我必把他沉到陀斐特。
谁都可以像约伯那样与神辩诉——虽然或许得不到同样的称义：他给我们说话的自由，必以绝对的公平垂听。但愿颂赞归神：凡这样就近他的人，唯一的结果必是——清清楚楚看见他确实正当，那完全的救主，甚至脱离他们自己存有之错谬的最深避难所，是的，永远比他们所能犯的任何错更近他们；这样看见他，他们就必厌恶自己、并在他里面喜乐。而且，如诗所指示的，当我们从自己转向他、变为真实——就是说，对神对我们自己都作我们所是的——他必转回我们的被掳；那带泪撒种的，必欢然收割；他们必欢欢喜喜地带禾捆回来。

===Original===

And, as the poem indicates, when we turn from ourselves to him, becoming true, that is, being to God and to ourselves what we are, he will turn again our captivity; they that have sown in tears shall reap in joy; they shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing their sheaves with them. Then will the waters that rise from God’s fountains, run in God’s channels.
For the prosperity that follows upon Job’s submission, is the embodiment of a great truth. Although a man must do right if it send him to Hades, yea, even were it to send him forever to hell itself, yet, while the Lord liveth, we need not fear: *all* good things must grow out of and hang upon the one central good, the one law of life﻿—the Will, the One Good. To submit absolutely to him is the only reason: circumstance as well as all being must then bud and blossom as the rose. And it will!﻿—what matter whether in this world or the next, if one day I know my life as a perfect bliss, having neither limitation nor hindrance nor pain nor sorrow more than it can dominate in peace and perfect assurance?
I care not whether the book of Job be a history or a poem. I think it is both﻿—I do not care how much relatively of each. It was probably, in the childlike days of the world, a well-known story in the east, which some man, whom God had made wise to understand his will and his ways, took up, and told after the fashion of a poet. What its age may be, who can certainly tell!﻿—it must have been before Moses. I would gladly throw out the part of Elihu as an interpolation. One in whom, of all men I have known, I put the greatest trust, said to me once what amounted to this: “There is as much difference between the language of the rest of the poem and that of Elihu, as between the language of Chaucer and that of Shakespeare.”
The poem is for many reasons difficult, and in the original to me inaccessible; but, through all the evident inadequacy of our translation, who can fail to hear two souls, that of the poet and that of Job, crying aloud with an agonized hope that, let the evil shows around them be what they may, truth and righteousness are yet the heart of things. The faith, even the hope of Job seems at times on the point of giving way; he struggles like a drowning man when the billow goes over him, but with the rising of his head his courage revives. Christians we call ourselves!

===Chinese===

那时，从神之泉源升起的众水，必流在神的河道里。
因为随着约伯的降服而来的兴盛，是一个伟大真理的化身。人虽然必须行义、哪怕它送他下阴间，是的、哪怕它永远送他下地狱本身，然而主活着，我们就无需惧怕：*一切*善物必从那独一的中央之善、那独一的生命之律——那旨意、那独一之善——生出并悬于其上。绝对顺服（obedience）于他，是唯一的理性：那时环境连同一切存有必发芽开花如玫瑰。而它必要如此！——至终有一日、我认识我的生命为完全的福乐、再没有它不能在平安与完全确握中驾驭的限制、拦阻、疼痛、忧伤，那时在今生还是来生，有什么要紧？
我不在乎《约伯记》是历史还是诗。我想两者都是——各占多少，我不在乎。它多半是，在世界还孩子气的日子，东方一个众所周知的故事，被某个神使他有智慧、能明白他旨意与他道路的人拿起来、照诗人的方式讲述了。它属什么年代，谁能确知！——必在摩西（Moses）之前。我乐意把以利户那段当作窜入之笔剔除。在我所认识的一切人中我最信_靠的那一位，曾对我说过一言，大意是：“全诗其余部分的语言与以利户的语言之间的差别，正如乔叟的语言与莎士比亚（Shakespeare）的语言之间的差别。”
这诗因许多缘故难解，原文于我也不可及；但透过我们译本一切显明的不足，谁听不见两个灵魂——诗人的与约伯的——以痛苦的盼望大声呼喊：任他们四周的恶显为怎样，真理与义（righteousness）仍是万事之心。约伯的信心、连他的盼望，有时似乎濒临崩溃；浪头盖过他时他像溺水的人挣扎，但头一浮起，勇气就复苏。我们自称基督徒！——若我们的信心比约伯的大、正如出自耶稣之口的话比他从旋风中所听的更有力量，我们的信心将要怎样！这里实在是一本信心之书，在律法借摩西赐下之前：恩典与真理已经造访我们——但我们的信心在哪里？

===Original===

﻿—what would not our faith be, were it as much greater than Job’s as the word from the mouth of Jesus is mightier than that he heard out of the whirlwind! Here is a book of faith indeed, ere the law was given by Moses: Grace and Truth have visited us﻿—but where is our faith?
Friends, our cross may be heavy, and the *via dolorosa* rough; but we have claims on God, yea the right to cry to him for help. He has spent, and is spending himself to give us our birthright, which is righteousness. Though we shall not be condemned for our sins, we cannot be saved but by leaving them; though we shall not be condemned for the sins that are past, we shall be condemned if we love the darkness rather than the light, and refuse to come to him that we may have life. God is offering us the one thing we cannot live without﻿—his own self: we must make room for him; we must cleanse our hearts that he may come in; we must do as the Master tells us, who knew all about the Father and the way to him﻿—*we must deny ourselves, and take up our cross daily, and follow him*.

===Chinese===

朋友们，我们的十架或许沉重，苦路（*via dolorosa*）或许崎岖；但我们对神有主张，是的、有向他呼求帮助的权利。他已倾尽、且正在倾尽自己，要给我们我们的长子名分——就是义。我们虽不至因我们的罪被定罪，却唯有离弃它们才能得救；我们虽不至为已过的罪被定罪，却必因爱黑暗过于爱光、拒绝到他那里得生命而被定罪。神正把他自己——我们没有它便活不成的那独一之物——献给我们：我们必须为他腾出空间；我们必须洁净我们的心、好叫他进来；我们必须照那位完全认识父与那路者的吩咐去行——*我们必须舍己，天天背起我们的十架，跟从他*。

### Self-Denial / 舍己
===Original===

> “And he said unto all, If any man would come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me. For whosoever would save his life shall lose it; but whosoever shall lose his life for my sake, the same shall save it.”

Christ is the way out, and the way in; the way from slavery, conscious or unconscious, into liberty; the way from the unhomeliness of things to the home we desire but do not know; the way from the stormy skirts of the Father’s garments to the peace of his bosom. To picture him, we need not only endless figures, but sometimes quite opposing figures: he is not only the door of the sheepfold, but the shepherd of the sheep; he is not only the way, but the leader in the way, the rock that followed, and the captain of our salvation. We must become as little children, and Christ must be born in us; we must learn of him, and the one lesson he has to give is himself: he does first all he wants us to do; he is first all he wants us to be. We must not merely do as he did; we must see things as he saw them, regard them as he regarded them; we must take the will of God as the very life of our being; we must neither try to get our own way, nor trouble ourselves as to what may be thought or said of us. The world must be to us as nothing.
I would not be misunderstood if I may avoid it: when I say “the world,” I do not mean the world God makes and means, yet less the human hearts that live therein; but the world man makes by choosing the perversion of his own nature﻿—a world apart from and opposed to God’s world. By “the world” I mean all ways of judging, regarding, and thinking, whether political, economical, ecclesiastical, social, or individual, which are not divine, which are not God’s ways of thinking, regarding, or judging; which do not take God into account, do not set his will supreme, as the one only law of life; which do not care for the truth of things, but the customs of society, or the practice of the trade; which heed not what is right, but the usage of the time. From everything that is against the teaching and thinking of Jesus, from the world in the heart of the best man in it, specially from the world in his own heart, the disciple must turn to follow him. The first thing in all progress is to leave something behind; to follow him is to leave one’s self behind. “If any man would come after me, let him deny himself.”

===Chinese===

> 耶稣又对众人说：若有人要跟从我，就当舍己，天天背起他的十架来跟从我。因为凡要救自己生命的，必丧掉生命；凡为我丧掉生命的，必救了生命。

基督是出路，也是入路；是脱离奴役——无论自觉与否——进入自由的路；是脱离事物的无家可归、进入我们所愿却还不认识的家之路；是脱离父衣袍风雨的边缘、进入他胸怀之平安的路。要描绘他，我们不但需要无尽的比喻，有时还须截然相反的比喻：他不仅是羊圈的门，也是羊的牧人；他不仅是道路，也是道路上的引领者、那随行的磐石、我们救恩的元帅。我们必须变成小孩子的样式，基督必须生在我们里面；我们必须跟他学，而他要给的唯一一课就是他自己：他先作一切他要我们作的；他先是一切他要我们成为的。我们不可仅照他所作的去作；我们必须照他看事物那样看事物、照他对待它们那样对待它们；我们必须把神的旨意（the will of God）当作我们存有的生命；我们既不可试图照自己的意思行，也不可烦恼别人会怎样想、怎样说我们。世界于我们必须如无有。
若能避免，我不要被误解：我说“世界”时，不是指神所造、所意味着的世界，更不是指活在其中的那些人心；而是指人因拣选自己天性的颠倒而造出的世界——一个离开神的世界、与它对立的世界。所谓“世界”，我指一切判断、看待、思考的方式——无论政治的、经济的、教会的、社会的、还是个人的——凡非属神的、非神的思想、看待、判断方式的；凡不把神计算在内、不立他的旨意为至尊、为生命唯一之律的；凡不顾事物的真实、只顾社会习俗或行业惯例的；凡不在意什么正当、只在意时下通行的。凡与耶稣的教导和思想相反的东西，连最好的人心里的世界——尤其自己心里的世界——门徒都必须转身离开、来跟从他。一切进步的第一件事，是把某物留在后面；跟从他，就是把自己留在后面。“若有人要跟从我，就当舍己（self-denial）。”

===Original===

Some seem to take this to mean that the disciple must go against his likings because they are his likings; must be unresponsive to the tendencies and directions and inclinations that are his, because they are such, and his; they seem to think something is gained by abstinence from what is pleasant, or by the doing of what is disagreeable﻿—that to thwart the lower nature is in itself a good. Now I will not dare say what a man may not get good from, if the thing be done in simplicity and honesty. I believe that when a man, for the sake of doing the thing that is right, does in mistake that which is not right, God will take care that he be shown the better way﻿—will perhaps use the very thing which is his mistake to reveal to him the mistake it is. I will allow that the mere effort of will, arbitrary and uninformed of duty, partaking of the character of tyranny and even schism, may add to the man’s power over his lower nature; but in that very nature it is God who must rule and not the man, however well he may mean. From a man’s rule of himself, in smallest opposition, however devout, to the law of his being, arises the huge danger of nourishing, by the pride of self-conquest, a far worse than even the unchained animal self﻿—the demoniac self. True victory over self is the victory of God in the man, not of the man alone. It is not subjugation that is enough, but subjugation by God. In whatever man does without God, he must fail miserably﻿—or succeed more miserably. No portion of a man can rule another portion, for God, not the man, created it, and the part is greater than the whole. In effecting what God does not mean, a man but falls into fresh ill conditions. In crossing his natural, therefore in themselves right inclinations, a man may develop a self-satisfaction which in its very nature is a root of all sin. Doing the thing God does not require of him, he puts himself in the place of God, becoming not a law but a lawgiver to himself, one who commands, not one who obeys. The diseased satisfaction which some minds feel in laying burdens on themselves, is a pampering, little as they may suspect it, of the most dangerous appetite of that self which they think they are mortifying.

===Chinese===

有人似乎把这理解为：门徒必须违逆自己的喜好，只因为那是他的喜好；必须对他的那些倾向、趋向、爱好不作回应，只因为它们是这样、是他的；他们似乎以为，戒绝愉快之事、或行不快之事，就算得了什么——以为挫抑低层天性本身就是善。我不敢说人不能从什么事得益，只要那事行在单纯与诚实里。我相信，当一个人为行正事之故、在错误中行了不正之事，神必看顾叫他看见更好的路——或许正借那件他的错误，向他显明它是错误。我承认，单凭意志的努力——任意而不识本分的、带着专横甚至分裂性质的——或能增加人对低层天性的驾驭；但在那天性里面，必须作王的是神，不是人，无论人用意多好。人凭自己对己的统治——哪怕在最微小的程度上违逆他存有之律，无论多么虔诚——就生出巨大的危险：借着克己的骄傲，养出一个比脱缰的兽性自我更坏的自我——那鬼魔性的自我。真正胜过自我，是神在人里面的胜利，不是人单独的胜利。单单征服还不够，必须是借神的征服。人无论作什么没有神的事，必悲惨地失败——或更悲惨地成功。人的任何一部分不能统治另一部分，因为是神而不是人造了它，且部分大于整体。人去成全神所不要的，只是落入新的恶境。人违逆自己的天然倾向——它们本身是正当的——或能培养出一种其本性即万恶之根的自满。人行神不要求于他的事，就把自己放在神的位置上，对自己不再是守法者、而成了立法者，成了发令者、不再是顺服者。有些人心中那种给自己加担子的病态满足，是他们所想苦待的那个自我之最危险食欲的娇养——他们自己还少有察觉。

===Original===

All the creatures of God are good, received with thanksgiving; then only can any one of them become evil, when it is used in relations in which a higher law forbids it, or when it is refused for the sake of self-discipline, in relations in which no higher law forbids, and God therefore allows it. For a man to be his own schoolmaster, is a right dangerous position; the pupil cannot be expected to make progress﻿—except, indeed, in the wrong direction. To enjoy heartily and thankfully, and do cheerfully without, when God wills we should, is the way to live in regard to things of the lower nature; these must nowise be confounded with the things of “the world.” If anyone say this is dangerous doctrine, I answer, “The law of God is enough for me, and for laws invented by man, I will none of them. They are false, and come all of rebellion. God and not man is our judge.”
Verily it is not to thwart or tease the poor self Jesus tells us. That was not the purpose for which God gave it to us! He tells us we must leave it altogether﻿—yield it, deny it, refuse it, lose it: thus only shall we save it, thus only have a share in our own being. The self is given to us that we may sacrifice it; it is ours that we like Christ may have somewhat to offer﻿—not that we should torment it, but that we should deny it; not that we should cross it, but that we should abandon it utterly: then it can no more be vexed.
“What can this mean?﻿—we are not to thwart, but to abandon? How abandon, without thwarting?”
It means this:﻿—we must refuse, abandon, deny self altogether as a ruling, or determining, or originating element in us. It is to be no longer the regent of our action. We are no more to think, “What should I like to do?” but “What would the Living One have me do?” It is not selfish to take that which God has made us to desire; neither are we very good to yield it﻿—we should only be very bad not to do so, when he would take it from us; but to yield it heartily, without a struggle or regret, is not merely to deny the Self a thing it would like, but to deny the Self itself, to refuse and abandon it. The Self is God’s making﻿—only it must be the “slave of Christ,” that the Son may make it also the free son of the same Father; it must receive all from him﻿—not as from nowhere; as well as the deeper soul, it must follow him, not its own desires.

===Chinese===

神的一切造物都是好的，都当存感谢的心领受；唯有当它被用在更高之律所禁止的关系中，或当它为了自律的缘故、在并无更高之律禁止、神因此容许的关系中被拒绝时，它才成为恶。人作自己的塾师，是很危险的处境；不能指望那学生进步——除了在错的方向上。当神愿我们享受时，就尽情而感恩地享受；当神愿我们无有，就甘心而没有它地过——这是对待低层之物的活法；这些绝不可与“世界”之物混为一谈。谁若说这是危险的教义，我回答：“神的律于我足够；人所发明的律，我一个也不要。它们是假的，都出于叛逆。审判我们的是神，不是人。”
真的，耶稣告诉我们的，不是要挫抑或戏弄那可怜的自我。那不是神把它赐给我们的目的！他告诉我们，必须全然把它撇下——交出它、否认它、拒绝它、失丧它：唯有这样我们才救得了它，唯有这样我们才在我们自己的存有中有份。自我赐给我们，是要我们把它献祭；它是我们的，好叫我们像基督那样有可献的——不是要我们折磨它，而是要我们否认它；不是要我们违逆它，而是要我们全然抛弃它：那时它就再不能被搅扰了。
“这能是什么意思？——不是违逆，而是抛弃？不违逆又怎样抛弃？”
意思是：——我们必须把自我全然拒绝、抛弃、否认，把它当作我们里面一个统治的、决定的、发端的元素。它不再是我们行动的摄政者。我们不再想“我愿作什么”，而想“那存活者愿我作什么”。取神使我们愿望的东西，不是自私；我们让出它也算不得很好——他若要把它从我们取去，我们不肯让才是很坏；但甘心情愿地让出它、毫无争扎或惋惜，就不只是否认自我一件它所愿的事，而是否认自我本身、拒绝并抛弃它。自我是神的造物——只是它必须作“基督的奴仆”，好叫子也使它作同一位父的自由之子；它必须从他领受一切——不是当作从无处来的；如那更深的灵魂一样，它必须跟从他，不是跟从自己的欲望。

===Original===

It must not be its own law; Christ must be its law. The time will come when it shall be so possessed, so enlarged, so idealized, by the indwelling God, who is its deeper, its deepest self, that there will be no longer any enforced denial of it needful; it has been finally denied and refused and sent into its own obedient place; it has learned to receive with thankfulness, to demand nothing; to turn no more upon its own centre, or any more think to minister to its own good. God’s eternal denial of himself, revealed in him who for our sakes in the flesh took up his cross daily, will have been developed in the man; his eternal rejoicing will be in God﻿—and in his fellows, before whom he will cast his glad self to be a carpet for their walk, a footstool for their rest, a stair for their climbing.
